intro: Morioka maps two trees, both national monuments and both born from disaster. Ishiwari-zakura, a cherry rooted in a cracked granite boulder at the district court, survived a 1932 fire when a gardener wrapped its trunk in his own wet coat. Twelve kilometres out at Ryugen-ji, a weeping katsura grows from a stump: the temple's original, over thirty metres tall, was felled for timber in 1824, and what stands now is the sucker that came up after. Both have carried National Natural Monument status since the 1920s.
meta_description: Morioka's two natural monuments: Ishiwari-zakura, a cherry splitting a granite boulder, and the weeping katsura regrown from a felled 1824 stump.
question_meta: Morioka's oldest tree is Ishiwari-zakura, the Rock-Splitting Cherry, growing from a granite boulder at the district court, with one more nearby.
question_answer: Morioka's oldest mapped tree is Ishiwari-zakura, the Rock-Splitting Cherry, an Edo Higan cherry rooted directly inside a crack in a large granite boulder on the grounds of Morioka District Court, judged to be roughly 350 to 420 years old.
question_context: The tree stands about 15 to 20 minutes on foot from JR Morioka Station, on the public grounds in front of the district courthouse, free daily (dogs must stay outside). Legend says lightning split the boulder and a cherry seed later caught in the crack; what is measured is a trunk about 4.3 metres round where it meets the stone. Japan designated it a National Natural Monument in 1923, among the earliest trees to receive that status. In 1932 a fire reached the courthouse; a gardener, Fujimura Jitaro, wrapped the trunk in his own wet coat rather than let it burn, and it bloomed again the following spring. It flowers for roughly ten days each April, and the court adds bus parking for the crowds. It is judged to be somewhere between 350 and 420 years old, a range rather than a fixed figure. About 12 kilometres out in Ohgayu, a second National Natural Monument, a weeping katsura at Ryugen-ji temple, grows from the stump of an older tree felled for timber in 1824.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Morioka?
faq.a: Ishiwari-zakura, the Rock-Splitting Cherry, an Edo Higan cherry judged to be roughly 350 to 420 years old, at Morioka District Court.

faq.q: Why does it grow out of a rock?
faq.a: Legend says lightning split the granite boulder and a cherry seed later lodged in the crack; nobody has established exactly how the tree ended up rooted there, but the trunk now measures about 4.3 metres round at the point where it meets the stone.

Yes, both trees. Ishiwari-zakura stands on the public grounds of Morioka District Court and is open to visitors daily (dogs must stay outside); the Ryugen-ji katsura stands on open temple grounds, no gate or fee.

faq.q: Is there another old tree in Morioka besides Ishiwari-zakura?
faq.a: Yes, about 12 kilometres out in the rural district of Ohgayu: a weeping katsura at Ryugen-ji temple, a National Natural Monument since 1924, that regrew from the stump of an even older tree felled for timber in 1824.
Ishiwari-zakura is about 15 to 20 minutes on foot from JR Morioka Station. The Ryugen-ji katsura is in Ohgayu, a rural district reached by car; there is no nearby station.

trees.name: Ishiwari-zakura (The Rock-Splitting Cherry)
trees.species: Edo Higan Cherry (Prunus itosakura, syn. Cerasus spachiana)

location.address: Uchimaru 9-1, grounds of Morioka District Court, Morioka, Iwate Prefecture, Japan

trees.access: Free, on the public grounds of the Morioka District Court in front of the courthouse building; open to visitors daily, dogs must stay outside the grounds. No ticket, appointment or reception needed.
trees.transport: About 15-20 minutes on foot from JR Morioka Station.
trees.story:
In 1932, fire tore through part of the Morioka District Court, and it looked as though it would take the cherry tree growing in the boulder in front of the building with it. A gardener named Fujimura Jitaro wrapped the trunk in his own wet coat rather than let it burn. It bloomed again the following spring.

The tree was already unusual before the fire. Legend says lightning split the granite boulder it grows from, and a cherry seed caught in the crack afterward, though nobody knows for certain how a tree ended up rooted half inside solid rock. What is certain is the result: a trunk about 4.3 metres round at the point where it meets the stone, forcing its way out of a fissure that offers it almost no soil.

Japan designated it a National Natural Monument in 1923, one of the earliest trees to receive that status, and the courthouse still keeps the grounds open daily so the public can walk up and see it, dogs excepted. It is judged to be somewhere between 350 and 420 years old, and every April, for the roughly ten days it is in bloom, the court adds bus parking for the crowds. A functioning court of law that also runs a car park for cherry blossoms is not a common combination, and it says something about how seriously the tree is taken here.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk forcing its way out of a crack in a large granite boulder, almost no soil visible at its base. It stands in front of the Morioka District Court building.

trees.name: Shidare Katsura of Ryugen-ji

location.address: Ryugen-ji temple, Ohgayu, Morioka City, Iwate Prefecture

trees.access: Free, on temple grounds (behind the main hall, at the edge of the graveyard); Ryugen-ji is an ordinary working Soto Zen temple, grounds open, no gate or booking involved
trees.transport: No station nearby; Ohgayu is a rural district outside central Morioka, reachable by car
trees.story:
The tree standing here exists because the one before it was cut up for the roof. By 1824 the old weeping katsura at Ryugen-ji had passed thirty metres, and the temple felled it for timber to repair the main hall. A sucker came up off the stump. That sucker is what you walk to now, about twenty-one metres tall and 3.5 metres round at chest height, and the two centuries it has been growing are the shortest part of its story.

The rest runs backwards. A weeping katsura, a rare variant of an otherwise ordinary species, was found growing wild in the mountains of Uchikawame roughly four hundred years ago. It was moved first to Myosen-ji, then moved again to Ryugen-ji by the priest who founded the temple in 1574. In 1924 Japan designated it a national Natural Monument together with two clonal sisters elsewhere in Morioka, all three counted as one monument under one name.

One thing to know about the numbers. The height and girth above come from a Morioka board of education sign put up in 1994, and every later source quotes that sign. It is one measurement repeated, not two that agree. A photograph from May 2018 shows the tree alive and in full leaf.

It grows behind the main hall at the edge of the graveyard, on the grounds of a working Soto Zen temple. No gate, no fee, and no station: Ohgayu is rural, and you arrive by car.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the weeping habit, branches hanging where an ordinary katsura's would spread, about twenty-one metres tall and 3.5 metres round. It stands behind the temple's main hall, at the edge of the graveyard.
